prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength, bringing the accuracy and stability of optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I change my preferred configuration from B057 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) to B027 alone (Katori and Ye). My round-1 reason for B057 was breadth of ranking and a stable, well-confirmed theory-plus-experiment story. Having read all eight statements and the chair's questions, I see that my own stated weakness for B057, the allocation of credit, was not answered by anyone, including me, and that is the criterion I used to set aside B054. Applying it consistently, B027 comes out ahead. It is a bounded invention with a before and after: the magic-wavelength condition lets many neutral atoms be interrogated without first-order light shift, Doppler or recoil, and the Katori and Ye groups showed that this route reaches uncertainties near 10^-18, confirmed by independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE). The magic-wavelength condition is at bottom a statement about calculated dynamic polarisabilities, which is the part of the argument I can follow from my own field, and Lindroth's point that it rests on non-trivial atomic structure persuades me that this is physics and not only engineering. On the chair's overlap question, the comb (2005) provided a way to count optical cycles and the 2012 prize concerned control of single quantum systems; neither contains the idea of holding an ensemble in a state where the clock transition is unperturbed, so I do not read the clock as a repeat. I also do not treat the unfinished redefinition of the second as a reason to wait: the performance is already independently demonstrated, and I would keep it out of the citation so the committee does not appear to anticipate a metrological decision. I would word the citation around the optical lattice clock itself, not optical clocks or precision spectroscopy in general. This is a change driven by credit and by the arguments of Lindroth, Danielsson, Mehlig and Kroll, not by the count of six supporters, which I do not regard as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against B027 is overlap with the 1997/2001, 2005 and 2012 prizes and the fact that much of its fundamental-physics reach (varying constants, dark matter, a redefined second, relativistic geodesy) is still prospective. Olsson's point that part of Ye's contribution is the pushing of accuracy rather than a distinct concept is fair, and I cannot rule it out from outside precision metrology. The two names also leave out ion-clock pioneers, other Sr and Yb lattice groups and ultrastable-laser developers, which is a real cost that a narrow citation reduces but does not remove. Separately, I leave B057 with regret: it is the broadest-ranked ballot and I still think the Z2 classification and the HgTe observation are first-rate physics, but a three-name credit that omits the proposers of the HgTe quantum spin Hall effect (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and the 3D contributors cannot, in my view, be repaired by citation wording alone, and the 2016 prize on topological phases narrows the room further.

responses.point: Lindroth holds B027 first because the magic-wavelength lattice is a specific idea with a specific demonstrator, the comb gave a way to count optical cycles while the lattice clock holds many atoms unperturbed, and the pending redefinition does not weaken the physics; she keeps B057 as the leading alternative.
responses.response: Your separation of the comb from the lattice clock is the argument that moved me on the overlap question, and your remark that polarisabilities, blackbody and higher-order light shifts make the physics deep gives me something I can check against my own electronic-structure experience. In round 1 I disagreed with you on ordering; I now accept it, for the reason you gave: I would not trade the clean B027 for a prize whose credit we cannot settle. I still would not call B057 overdue, but that no longer affects my position.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B027 first for its bounded shape, a clear before and after and a two-person credit, wants the citation to name the clock itself, and keeps B057 and B041 as alternatives while noting the 2016 overlap and credit disputes for B057.
responses.response: I agree with the wording requirement and have written my citation around the lattice clock and the 10^-18 level, not around metrology generally. On B057 you and I read the 2016 overlap the same way, as narrower than the whole of topological matter but still a reason for care. I used to say the contested credit does not make the science weaker; that remains true, but a prize has to cite specific names, and the HgTe-proposal gap is the issue I could not answer when the chair asked whether the citation can withstand the omissions.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B027 because its attribution is unusually clean compared with the compromised alternatives, argued that a measurement-science prize is not lesser science, and would put the citation in terms of the invention, not its applications such as the second redefinition.
responses.response: I accept your framing, including the statistical-physics point that the many-body Fermi-gas operation of the clock makes it more than an instrument. You also rejected B054 for Metzner's omission, and the same fairness test applies to B057; I should have applied it to my own preferred ballot in round 1. I agree the citation should be about the invention and not commit the committee to the outcome of the redefinition of the second.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, moved from IceCube to B027, concedes that overlap with the comb and ion-trap prizes is the strongest argument against it, and gives less weight to the prospective reach than to the instrument case.
responses.response: I agree with giving the prospective applications little weight; the case for B027 stands on what has been demonstrated and reproduced. On your overlap concession I would add that the 1e-18 result is a different physical route from the ion clocks, so the magic-wavelength lattice is not the same achievement. On B041 I said in round 1 that I would defer to you and Danielsson on whether Halzen and Karle are decisive, and nothing in the exchange changes that; I note that you yourself say the credit cannot be defended as supplied, so I do not support it as a part.

responses.point: Kroll argues for a narrow lattice-clock citation, notes that Al+ and other ion-clock results come from groups outside the credited names and that this is an attribution cost, and would not combine B027 with B032.
responses.response: I agree that widening the citation to ion clocks would force the committee to adjudicate between different physical arguments and different people, and I would accept the cost of leaving them out. I also agree there is no workable second part: with Katori and Ye taking two of three places, a second achievement would have to be credited to one person, and none of the shortlisted candidates splits that way fairly. I therefore propose B027 alone.

responses.point: Olsson lists B027 as an alternative, says the 2005 prize covers much of the enabling frequency metrology, and thinks Ye's contribution is partly the pushing of accuracy rather than a distinct concept; her own first choice, B053, is an enabling instrument she would not insist on.
responses.response: I take the point about Ye seriously and cannot dismiss it from outside metrology. My answer is that the credit pairs the originator of the concept with the group that demonstrated what it can reach and made it a general tool, which is a conventional and fair structure. On B053, I cannot judge instrument credit in electron optics, and the Krivanek omission and her own proximity disclosure make it harder than the clock, though I respect that she has put the case honestly.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-ion prizes; I rely on Lindroth, Danielsson and Kroll for the metrology, since it is outside my expertise.
Whether the exclusion of ion-clock pioneers, early Sr and Yb lattice groups and ultrastable-laser developers will be judged unfair even with a narrow citation.
Whether Ye's contribution is a distinct idea or mainly the extension of accuracy, as Olsson suggests.
Whether my change from B057 reflects the weight of the credit problem or deference to colleagues in a field I cannot judge; I have tried to apply the same fairness test to B027, B054 and B057.
My recollection of priority dates in the HgTe and 3D topological insulator literature is from memory and not verified here.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B027, and my profile lists no relationship with Katori, Ye or their groups. B054 (DMFT) and B057 (spin-orbit band topology), which I now hold as alternatives, lie close to my own electronic-structure research, a topical proximity and not a documented personal or institutional connection. This is unchanged from round 1 and does not require recusal.
